title: Filipino Myths: Gods, Giants and the Lost City — Part 2
titleOptions: Filipino Myths: Gods, Giants and the Lost City — Part 2
Filipino Gods and Legends: The Myths They Tried to Erase — Part 2
Bathala, the Moon Goddess and the Vanishing City — Filipino Mythology Part 2
hook: Before colonizers ever reached these islands, the Philippines already had a heaven, a creation story, and gods of its own. Tonight we meet them — Bathala, the moon goddess who lost an eye, a giant still holding up two mountains, and a golden city that vanishes at dawn.

scenes.text: Before the galleons and the crosses, before anyone called these islands the Philippines, they already had a heaven. May langit na sila. May mga diyos na sila. Gods who shaped the sea, giants who held up mountains, and a city of gold in the jungle. Ito ang ating mitolohiya. Ngayong gabi, makikilala natin ang mga diyos.

scenes.text: Last time, we walked the dark side of these islands — the Bakunawa that devours the moon, the manananggal, the aswang, the tikbalang on the road. Ngunit hindi puro takot ang kuwentong Pilipino. But Filipino stories are not only fear. Above the monsters stood the gods — older, greater, and waiting five hundred years for someone to tell their story.

scenes.text: In the memory of the Tagalog people, one god stood above all the rest: Bathala, maker of heaven and earth. Naninirahan siya sa Kaluwalhatian, the shining kingdom above the clouds. Below him stretched only sea, sky, and wind. Wala pang lupa. Wala pang tao. Wala pang buhay. Only a god, looking at an empty world, deciding what it would become.

scenes.text: But the sea and the sky were enemies, and their war tore the world apart. Naghahagis ng bato ang langit. Nagbabaon ng alon ang dagat. The sky hurled mountains down; the sea threw its waves back. The rocks became islands — libo-libong piraso ng isang sirang mundo, thousands of pieces of a broken world. And on one shore, bamboo waited.

scenes.chapterTitle: Apolaki and Mayari: When the Sun Fought the Moon
scenes.text: A kingdom needs heirs, and Bathala's own children could not share the sky. Apolaki, god of the sun, burned with pride and fire. Si Mayari naman, diyosa ng buwan, shone with a cooler and gentler light. Pareho silang gustong maghari sa langit. Both of them wanted the heavens. And neither child of Bathala would ever kneel to the other.

scenes.text: So brother and sister went to war. Araw laban sa buwan. Apoy laban sa pilak. Sun against moon, fire against silver, their battle raged until the sky shook. Then, in a moment of fury, Apolaki struck — at nasugatan niya ang mata ng kanyang kapatid. He had wounded his sister's eye. And his pride died there in the light.

The gods, our ancestors said, can wound what they love — and still choose to make it right.

scenes.chapterTitle: Maria Makiling, Guardian of the Mountain
scenes.text: Drive from Manila and you will see her sleeping: the mountain of Los Baños, Laguna, shaped like a woman lying down. Bundok Makiling. But the old people shake their heads — that is no mountain. Iyon ay isang diwata. That is a fairy named Maria Makiling, guardian of the forests, the deer, and every traveler who climbs her slopes.

scenes.chapterTitle: Bernardo Carpio, the Giant Between Two Mountains
scenes.text: Hindi lahat ng higante sa ating kuwento ay diyos — not every giant is a god. In Montalban, Rizal, they tell of Bernardo Carpio, a boy of the Spanish days with impossible strength. Kaya niyang bumuhat ng malaking bato na parang unan lamang. He could shoulder a boulder the way you carry a pillow.

scenes.text: A hero that strong could not be fought — so he was tricked. Inilayo siya sa isang bangin sa Wawa, and with magic, enemies sprang the trap: the two mountains crashed together to crush him. Ngunit itinaas ni Bernardo ang kanyang mga kamay. But Bernardo raised his arms — and caught them. He is holding them apart to this day.

scenes.text: Now fly south, to Mindanao, to the Maranao people of Lake Lanao — and meet the most radiant bird in all our legends: the Sarimanok. Balahibo nitong kumikinang sa lahat ng kulay ng bukang-liwayway. Its feathers blaze with every color of the dawn, and it carries a fish in its beak. scenes.text: Some cities are lost to history. One city in Samar refuses to be found. Its name is Biringan. Sa ilang gabi, isinusumpa ng mga mangingisda na nakikita nila ito — on certain nights, fishermen swear they see it from the sea: towers of light rising out of the jungle, streets shining like gold. By morning, wala na. It is gone.

scenes.text: Its people, they say, are engkanto — tall, beautiful, and not quite human, dressed like Spanish nobles of another age. Truck drivers in Samar still swear they delivered goods to an address that no map has ever held. At ang mga naimbitahan papasok? And those invited inside say one shining night in Biringan can steal years from the world outside.

scenes.text: Search parties have crossed that jungle and found only trees. Walang kalsada. Walang gusali. No roads. No buildings. Some doors, our ancestors knew, open only from the other side.

scenes.chapterTitle: The Babaylan: Keepers of the Old World
scenes.text: One last thing before we go: every story tonight survived because someone refused to stop telling it. Before the Spanish came, that someone was the babaylan — pari, manggagamot, at tagapag-ingat ng lumang mundo: priestess, healer, and keeper of the old world. Sila ang tulay — they were the bridge between the villages and the gods you have just met.
